newsitem.title: USA: New York brokers plead guilty to forgery.
newsitem.headline: New York brokers plead guilty to forgery.

text.p: Thirty stockbrokers who were accused of involvement in the biggest securities license scam in Wall Street history struck a plea bargain on Tuesday to avoid jail on forgery charges, prosecutors said.

The stockbrokers, who were accused of paying imposters to take tests administered by the National Association of Securities Dealers (NASD), could have been imprisoned for up to 4 years for the forgery charges but instead will pay fines ranging from $5,000 to $20,000.
The defendants also agreed to lifetime disbarment from the NASD and will be prohibited from trading in New York State.

The case against 23 other defendants who were arrested last month is still pending. They include four alleged middleman and two ringers who are accused of taking the tests for the brokers. A 54th stockbroker pleaded guilty in January.

The indictment of the brokers last month revealed that the men worked at 17 small and medium-size brokerage firms including Stratton Oakmont, Hanover Sterling & Co., A.S. Goldmen & Co., and Gruntal & Co.

Evidence uncovered during the 2-1/2-year investigation revealed that the indicted brokers paid imposters up to $5,000 or were promised future shares of commissions, in exchange for taking the tests for them between 1993 and 1995, prosecutors said.
The investigation began in 1994 when an examination proctor noticed the same person taking multiple tests under a number of different names.
Brokers must pass a series of licensing examinations administered by the NASD at its 56 centres nationwide before they can sell securities to investors.
The 6-hour test measures a person's knowledge of securities issues, markets, regulations and laws. New York State also requires an additional exam to qualify as a stockbroker.
Some of the stockbrokers had previously failed the exhaustive examination, Manhattan District Attorney Robert Morgenthau said.
